source.title: On the Generalization Benefit of Noise in Stochastic Gradient Descent
source.authors: Samuel L. Smith; Erich Elsen; Soham De

record.tranche_reason: Sweeps batch size under fixed epoch and step budgets, with tuned learning rates, and measures held-out performance; it tests a batch-size condition in V5 rather than the claim’s memorization premise.
record.gate_note: The study also compares SGD with and without momentum and measures training loss/perplexity, but does not test adaptive optimizers, memorization of random labels, model width, or the listed sharpness and example-removal measures. Values used only to characterize optimal learning rates are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: Tests V5 through batch-size sweeps with learning-rate searches, reporting held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and complementary fixed step budgets. The latter give larger batches more epochs and test whether the penalty persists with additional training. This study is not an original source listed for V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but incomplete. The authors conclude that small or moderately large batches can outperform very large batches after learning-rate tuning under both fixed epoch and fixed step budgets. In some fixed step comparisons the larger batches achieve lower training loss, supporting a generalization benefit from gradient noise. They also find evidence that noise early in training matters, and explicitly restrict their conclusions to the schedules and architectures studied.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps batch size and tunes learning rates for SGD with and without Momentum, measuring test performance under fixed epoch and step budgets; it does not test all training recipes or the claim’s memorization premise.
record.method_sensitivity: Held-out performance varies with batch size, compute budget, dataset, architecture, normalization, and optimizer (vanilla SGD versus Momentum). The observed batch-size threshold differs by model and setting.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST autoencoder reconstruction MSE rises weakly with batch size under fixed steps, from 2.91 to 2.98; fixed-epoch reconstruction also deteriorates beyond optimizer-dependent thresholds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Large-batch training can worsen held-out reconstruction performance in autoencoders.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed batch size, longer training can saturate or worsen held-out performance, while learning rates optimal for held-out performance differ from those optimal for training loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training duration and the early learning-rate schedule affect generalization independently of minimizing training loss.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: The authors limit their conclusions to the learning-rate schedule and architectures studied. ResNet-50/ImageNet entries use a single run per batch-size/learning-rate pair, without error bars. Several additional results are described only qualitatively from figures.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the extracted test-performance sweeps. Training loss/perplexity measures reported alongside the test metrics were not separately rowed; the text and tables use them as supporting comparisons to test performance.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization in the same training setup.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning and recovery strategies.

Controlled warmup and regularization remedies, exhaustive schedule tuning, and whether sufficiently long or differently scheduled training can eliminate each observed penalty. Fixed step sweeps give large batches more epochs but do not establish the best attainable performance over training durations.
Dropout interventions; using dropout in the LSTM is not a test of its benefit.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.

missing.what: Fixed-epoch PTB LSTM batch-size results: test perplexity rises above batch 64 for vanilla SGD and above 128 for Momentum, after learning-rate searches, using the best five of seven runs.

record.verdict_notes: Fixed step results bear on persistence of the penalty with additional training, not on an equal-epoch comparison. Intermediate batch-size optima are consistent with V5's workload-dependent threshold. Training-loss rows were explicitly declared omitted, so they are not listed as missing. Learning rates were selected using test performance; Wide-ResNet summaries use the best 12 of 15 runs, and LSTM summaries the best five of seven. Several source captions mistakenly say maximize perplexity or MSE; the surrounding analysis establishes minimization as the intended objective.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning effects.

No explicit comparison of large-batch recipe changes such as longer training, warmup, or normalization/regularization changes as remedies; experiments do include both normalized and unnormalized models.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.

reader_labels.reason: Test accuracy is highest at an intermediate batch size, then drops at larger batches; the CIFAR-100 unnormalized sweep also reports a large training-loss standard deviation and does not show a uniformly falling training loss (R12-R16, R26-R30).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Fixed step budget, PTB word-level LSTM; MNIST autoencoder
reader_labels.reason: The batch-size relationship depends on model and metric: PTB test perplexity is lowest at batch size 64 and worsens at both smaller and larger sizes, while the autoencoder’s test MSE changes only weakly with batch size (R31-R39).

reader_labels.condition: Constant epoch budget, CIFAR-10 16-4 Wide-ResNet; ImageNet ResNet-50
reader_labels.reason: With fixed epochs, held-out performance begins to degrade past a model-dependent batch threshold; on ResNet-50 the table values are single runs and the small-batch differences are described as equal (R40-R41, R44-R49).
